Meat Offering
MEET OFF-er-ing
n. phrase
Meat in older English meant any food (not specifically flesh); the KJV uses meat offering for the Hebrew minōchāh, “tribute, present, grain offering,” which was actually a flour-and-oil grain offering, not a flesh sacrifice. Modern translations correctly render grain offering.

📖 Biblical Definition

The meat offering of the KJV is the grain offering of modern translations—the Hebrew minōchāh, an offering of fine flour mixed with oil and frankincense, baked or fried into cakes or wafers, prescribed in Leviticus 2 and offered as an accompaniment to most of the other sacrifices. The KJV’s meat here is the older English word meaning food in general (compare green meat for vegetables, nutmeat for the edible kernel); modern English having narrowed meat to flesh of slaughtered animals, the KJV translation now misleads the modern reader. Several structural features mark the doctrine. First, the materials: fine flour (the staple food of life), oil (the substance of consecration and the Spirit’s anointing), frankincense (the substance of prayer ascending to the LORD), and salt (the substance of covenant—neither shalt thou suffer the salt of the covenant of thy God to be lacking from thy meat offering, Lev 2:13). No leaven and no honey were to be used (Lev 2:11)—leaven typifying corruption-by-spread and honey typifying sweetness-without-substance. Second, the procedure: the offerer brought his offering to the priest, who took a memorial portion and burned it on the altar; the rest belonged to the priests as most holy of the offerings of the LORD made by fire (Lev 2:3). Third, the function: the meat offering typically accompanied the burnt offering and peace offering, not as a substitutionary atonement (the meat offering had no blood) but as an offering of devotion, tribute, and the firstfruits of the offerer’s labor. The flour and oil represented the offerer’s work (cultivation, harvest, milling, baking); the offering presented to the LORD the labor of the offerer’s hands as devoted to Him. Fourth, the typological substance. The meat offering with its no-leaven, no-honey, with-oil, with-salt particulars points toward Christ in His perfect humanity: fine flour without leaven (no corruption); anointed with oil (the Spirit without measure); seasoned with salt of the covenant (the unchanging fidelity to the Father’s purposes); offered without honey (no merely-sweet sentimentality but the substance of righteousness). Christ’s life of perfect devotion to the Father, offered as a continual minōchāh, is the substance the OT grain offering anticipated; and through Christ, the saint’s own labor and devotion are accepted before the LORD as a spiritual sacrifice well-pleasing to God (Heb 13:15-16; 1 Pet 2:5).

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 notes that MEAT in older English denoted any food, and the KJV’s MEAT OFFERING is the Hebrew minōchāh, an offering of fine flour mixed with oil and frankincense, prescribed in Leviticus 2; modern translations correctly render grain offering.

expand to see more

MEAT, n. — 1. Food in general; any thing eaten for nourishment, whether of man or beast. 2. The flesh of animals used as food. (The narrower modern sense.) 3. In scripture, the KJV uses meat offering for the Hebrew grain-and-flour offering (Lev 2).

OFFERING, n. — 1. The act of offering. 2. That which is offered; that which is presented in divine service. 3. In scripture, the various OT sacrifices and presentations to the LORD, including the burnt offering, peace offering, sin offering, trespass offering, meat (grain) offering, drink offering, and the like.

📖 Key Scripture

Leviticus 2:1-2 — "And when any will offer a meat offering unto the LORD, his offering shall be of fine flour; and he shall pour oil upon it, and put frankincense thereon: And he shall bring it to Aaron’s sons the priests: and he shall take thereout his handful of the flour thereof, and of the oil thereof, with all the frankincense thereof; and the priest shall burn the memorial of it upon the altar..."

Leviticus 2:11 — "No meat offering, which ye shall bring unto the LORD, shall be made with leaven: for ye shall burn no leaven, nor any honey, in any offering of the LORD made by fire."

Leviticus 2:13 — "And every oblation of thy meat offering shalt thou season with salt; neither shalt thou suffer the salt of the covenant of thy God to be lacking from thy meat offering: with all thine offerings thou shalt offer salt."

Hebrews 13:15-16 — "By him therefore let us offer the sacrifice of praise to God continually, that is, the fruit of our lips giving thanks to his name. But to do good and to communicate forget not: for with such sacrifices God is well pleased."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The meat-offering doctrine is corrupted primarily by the KJV-translation drift in modern English: meat no longer means food generally but specifically flesh, so the modern reader of the KJV encounters meat offering and forms an incorrect picture (a flesh offering rather than a grain offering)—and by the general loss of typological reading that has dropped the meat/grain offering from contemporary preaching as obscure ritual detail.

expand to see more

The KJV-translation drift is the most concrete contemporary corruption of the meat-offering doctrine. Meat in 1611 English meant food in general; meat offering was therefore a perfectly natural rendering of the grain-and-oil-and-frankincense offering Leviticus prescribes. In modern English, meat has narrowed to flesh of slaughtered animals, with the result that the modern reader of the KJV forms an incorrect picture: a flesh offering rather than the grain offering Scripture actually describes. The remedy is partly translational (modern translations have correctly rendered grain offering) and partly catechetical (KJV readers should be taught that meat in the KJV often means food generally, as in strong meat belongeth to them that are of full age in Heb 5:14, which clearly means strong food, not strong flesh). The KJV’s antique vocabulary is rich and rewarding but requires this kind of careful attention to the language-shift over four centuries.

The deeper corruption is the general loss of typological reading that has dropped the meat/grain offering from contemporary preaching as obscure ritual detail without typological substance. The grain offering, with its no-leaven (no corruption), no-honey (no merely-sweet sentimentality), oil (the Spirit’s anointing), and salt (the covenant’s fidelity) particulars, typifies Christ in His perfect humanity and the substance of His life of devotion to the Father. The recovery is the recovery of the typology: the OT sacrifices were the appointed shadows of which Christ is the substance; the grain offering particularly points to the substance of Christ’s perfect humanity offered in devotion to the Father, and to the spiritual sacrifices of praise and good works the saint now offers through Him (Heb 13:15-16). The contemporary preacher who skips Leviticus 2 misses one of the more pastorally tender of the OT typologies; the recovery of typological reading restores the doctrinal substance and the spiritual application alike.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew minōchāh (tribute, present, grain offering); the OT grain offering of fine flour, oil, frankincense, and salt prescribed in Leviticus 2 as the offering of devotion, tribute, and firstfruits-labor; typologically anticipating Christ’s perfect-humanity life of devotion to the Father and the spiritual sacrifices the saint now offers through Him.

expand to see more

Hebrew minōchāh (H4503) — tribute, present, grain offering (over 200 OT uses).

Hebrew qōrbān (H7133) — an offering brought near to God (the general OT word for offering).

Greek thusia (G2378) — sacrifice, offering (NT term).

Greek prosphora (G4376) — offering, presentation (Heb 10:10, 14, 18).

Usage

"The KJV meat offering = the Hebrew minōchāh = the grain offering of fine flour, oil, frankincense, and salt; meat in 1611 English meant food generally."

"The grain offering’s no-leaven, no-honey, with-oil, with-salt particulars typify Christ’s perfect humanity offered in devotion to the Father."

"KJV-language-drift produces misreading (meat now means flesh, but the offering was grain); loss of typology drops the doctrine; recovery is translation-attention and typological reading together."
